name: Acuity Scheduling
tagline: Client booking, intake forms, payments, reminders, and classes

pricing.notes: Working normalization from the official public pricing structure. Recheck the source page immediately before publication.

tiers.name: Starter
tiers.limits: 1 calendar, unlimited services and appointments, intake forms and email reminders

tiers.name: Standard
tiers.limits: Up to 6 calendars; text reminders; packages, memberships and gift certificates

tiers.name: Premium
tiers.limits: Up to 36 calendars; HIPAA BAA, removed branding, multiple time zones, API and custom CSS

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Unlimited calendars, unlimited scheduling instances, additional APIs and VIP account management

pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual (about 20% off); 7-day trial, no credit card
pricing.hiddenCosts: Taxes and ordinary payment-processor fees are extra. Calendar limits are hard plan differentiators; there are no setup, cancellation or support fees on self-serve plans.

verdictSummary: The visible appointment scheduling loop is buildable, but a credible replacement needs more than the first screen. Acuity Scheduling earns its keep through OAuth, calendar reliability, so expect a weekend or multi-day build and a narrower personal scope.
coreLoopDIY: Build a personal appointment scheduling tool that reads one calendar, publishes availability, reserves a slot, and writes the event back.
replacementScope: narrow personal or very small-team substitute
whatYouLose: reliable reminders and timezone edge cases
calendar-provider edge cases and timezone correctness
whyPeopleStillPay: Acuity Scheduling: People pay because a booking tool must never double-book them, leak private events, or send the wrong time to a client.
ongoingBurden: Maintain OAuth, timezone data, webhooks, idempotency, reminders, calendar-provider quirks, and uptime.

priorArt.name: Cal.com
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source scheduling platform and OAuth reference.

alternatives.name: Appointy Free
alternatives.desc: One staffer gets reminders, classes and Square checkout for 100 bookings a month; growth wakes the paywall.

facts.dataFormat: Booking, customer, service and staff records live in Appointy's cloud, with connected calendar and payment data also handled by their respective providers
facts.gapVsPaid: The 100-appointment cap and five-service limit arrive quickly, while advanced intake, packages, subscriptions and payment options are thinner than Acuity's.

alternatives.name: Setmore Free
alternatives.desc: Four staff, payments, classes and 200 monthly bookings; SMS, recurring appointments and two-way sync cost extra.

facts.dataFormat: Booking, customer and staff records live in Setmore's cloud, with calendar and payment records also passing through connected providers
facts.gapVsPaid: The free plan stops at 200 appointments and omits recurring appointments, SMS reminders, two-way sync and Acuity's advanced intake and package tools.

alternatives.name: Square Appointments Free
alternatives.desc: A serious free solo booking stack where Square operates; processing fees remain and the feature mix varies by country.

facts.install: Create or use a Square seller account and enable Appointments
facts.dataFormat: Appointment, customer, staff and transaction records live in Square's cloud
facts.gapVsPaid: The free plan is solo and country-dependent, ties payments to Square processing and leaves more advanced team and resource features paid.
facts.setupBlocker: A Square seller account and identity verification, and the service must be available in the user's country

alternatives.name: zcal Free
alternatives.desc: Forms, Stripe payments, email reminders and group classes are free; teams are paid and zcal takes 3%.

facts.dataFormat: Account and booking records live in zcal's cloud; Stripe processes and stores payment details for paid bookings
facts.gapVsPaid: It lacks Acuity's client records, packages, subscriptions and class administration; teams are paid and Stripe payments carry a 3% commission.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Easy!Appointments
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Everyone points here for open source; it has providers and reminders, but no built-in payments or class workflow.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Picktime Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The free plan handles classes and bookings, but reminders and custom intake fields are paid.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Reservio Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Free means 40 bookings a month and no calendar sync; that is a demo-sized business, not a replacement.

notes: Useful boundary case: the first 60 percent of Acuity Scheduling is approachable, but operating the last 40 percent is the real subscription.
prompt:
Build a deliberately narrow personal substitute for Acuity Scheduling, not a full clone.
Use exactly this stack: Next.js 15 + TypeScript + SQLite.
Primary job: Build a personal appointment scheduling tool that reads one calendar, publishes availability, reserves a slot, and writes the event back.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: race-free booking under load; team routing and round robin; reliable reminders and timezone edge cases.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
